components.text: Explain why the evidence for God or Christian claims is sufficiently plausible to warrant belief.
Whether the evidence for God and Christian claims is sufficiently plausible to warrant belief.
Show that the cited biblical examples portray faith as belief contrary to evidence rather than trust informed by prior reasons.
Whether Thomas and Abraham exemplify belief contrary to evidence rather than trust grounded in prior reasons.
Provide a non-arbitrary way to distinguish Christianity from rival religious truth claims.
Whether Christianity can be non-arbitrarily privileged when rival religious worldviews make competing claims.
Explain why Christian supernatural claims receive warranted preference over competing religious claims.
Supply a structured body of evidence capable of making Christian belief plausible rather than merely possible.
Show that Christian belief proceeds from evidence rather than requiring belief contrary to it.
Whether Christianity has a non-arbitrary evidential advantage over competing religious revelations.
Whether Christian belief has a sufficiently plausible evidential basis rather than merely subjective experience.
Apply non-arbitrary comparative criteria when preferring the Christian miracle claim over rival explanations and traditions.
Explain how available evidence can make a supernatural conclusion comparatively plausible.
Demonstrate an evidence-sensitive rather than evidence-opposed method of Christian inference.
Whether Christian supernatural claims are non-arbitrarily privileged over competing religious claims.
Whether Christian claims can be assessed through plausibility and explanatory evidence rather than dismissed categorically.
Show that the accumulated evidence makes resurrection comparatively superior rather than merely immune from advance exclusion.
Defend the appearance reports and martyr traditions required by the proposed cumulative resurrection sequence.
Whether the accumulated historical evidence supplies enough discriminating force to warrant resurrection over rival explanations.
Whether appearance testimony, the empty tomb, and martyr traditions complete the proposed staged resurrection case.
Explain why a God seeking human recognition and relationship does not disclose himself more clearly to sincere nonbelievers.
Explain why stronger direct experiential evidence is not supplied when current evidence seems implausible.
Why God would withhold unmistakable disclosure from sincere nonbelievers who seek recognizable knowledge of God.
Explain how scriptural authority or theological usability survives textual variation and potentially lost wording.
Show that accepting Scripture need not require trust contrary to transmission evidence.
Whether textual variation and possible loss defeat the preservation and theological usability of Scripture.
Show that Christian or theistic belief is supported by evidence rather than accepted with no evidence.
State criteria for deciding whether the evidence supporting a worldview is sufficiently plausible.
Provide non-arbitrary comparative standards for choosing among competing worldviews.
Address whether textual variants undercut the comparative evidence for Christianity.
Whether theistic belief has evidence sufficient to make it rationally comparable with skeptical or naturalistic alternatives.
Whether competing worldviews can be distinguished through non-arbitrary public criteria.
Whether rational faith may be grounded in evidence rather than accepted without evidence.
Explain why the narrated tongues and conversion experiences require or support an external divine cause.
Show that a biblical historical tradition remains usable despite textual and transmission concerns.
Whether religious experiences can be explained by social and psychological mechanisms without divine causation.
Whether biblical texts remain historically usable despite challenges to transmission and textual privilege.
Show that a historical Exodus model remains evidentially credible despite the narrative's enormous population figures.
Explain how the scriptural message remains trustworthy when numerical reporting appears historically implausible.
Whether a historically credible minimal Exodus remains supported despite tensions between the narrative and archaeological-demographic evidence.
Whether the cited biblical evidence is sufficient to ground faith rather than require trust despite weak evidence.
Explain how the Exodus population figures can remain historically or literarily usable despite conflict with ancient demographic estimates.
Explain why ancient textual differences should be interpreted within their original cultural conventions.
Whether implausibly large Exodus figures undermine historical trust even if they are described as hyperbolic.
Justify reliance on culturally specialized interpretive conventions when God purportedly intends Scripture to reveal truth broadly.
Explain why divine preservation would operate through a message whose interpretation is confusing and expert-dependent.
Show that the proposed minimal historical reading is accessible rather than dependent on contested scholarly reconstruction.
Whether culturally specific ancient conventions adequately preserve an accessible and trustworthy meaning for modern readers.
Whether message-level preservation is adequate when interpretation requires extensive specialist knowledge.
Show that appeals to ancient cultural convention do not become selective devices for protecting Christian claims.
Assess Christianity's historical claims against the wider ancient cultural and religious environment.
Apply public worldview comparison to pre-Christian miracle, exaltation, death, and return traditions.
Whether ancient numerical conventions answer the demographic conflict in the Exodus account.
Whether Christian resurrection claims remain comparatively distinctive against broader ancient religious patterns.
Explain why nonidentical pre-Christian miracle, exaltation, death, return, or resurrection parallels should not reduce confidence in Christian distinctiveness.
Provide non-arbitrary comparative criteria distinguishing Christianity from rival traditions.
Show that Christian resurrection evidence remains comparatively stronger despite contested testimony and analogous claims.
Whether broad pre-Christian similarities should reduce confidence in the distinctiveness of the Christian resurrection claim.
Whether Christianity can be distinguished from rival traditions using public comparative criteria.
Explain how divine inspiration and revelation remain credible when ancient conventions produce discrepancies and interpretive difficulty.
Explain why textual discrepancies and nonexact wording do not defeat scriptural inspiration.
Explain why numerical conflict need not defeat the historical or theological usability of Scripture.
Explain why ancient literary and religious similarities do not reduce Scripture to ordinary cultural production.
Whether confusing culturally distant texts are compatible with a God who preserves and reveals an understandable message.
Whether discrepancies and textual differences defeat scriptural preservation and theological usability.
Provide a positive reason to infer divine inspiration once discrepancies and culturally conditioned human authorship are conceded.
Show why sincere fallible transmission requires divine agency rather than ordinary human belief and composition.
Explain why culturally specific conventions evidence inspiration rather than ordinary ancient authorship.
Distinguish scriptural divine agency from ordinary culturally available religious explanation.
Whether a fallibilist inspiration model explains Scripture better than ordinary culturally situated human composition.
Whether divine agency is needed to explain sincere ancient authors and message-level transmission.
Explain why fallibilist and culturally conditioned testimony can warrant an exceptional resurrection claim.
Include the strong ordinary-experience prior against bodily resurrection in comparative hypothesis assessment.
Show that the cumulative case overcomes repeated ordinary experience that dead people remain dead.
Explain why prior testimonial and textual evidence should outweigh the induction against resurrection.
State what case-specific evidence could warrant resurrection rather than ordinary explanations.
Whether resurrection is comparatively warranted despite its conflict with extensive ordinary experience of death's permanence.
Whether faith in resurrection is grounded in sufficient evidence rather than opposed by stronger ordinary evidence.
Whether direct divine disclosure could rationally resolve sincere nonbelief without forcing love or worship.
